history.heading: Islands of the Moon
paragraphs: The Comoros are a volcanic archipelago in the Mozambique Channel between Madagascar and East Africa. The islands were settled by Bantu-speaking Africans, Austronesians and later Arab and Persian traders. Their Arabic name, Juzur al-Qamar, means "Islands of the Moon".

Islam arrived early, and the islands became part of the Swahili trading world, ruled by competing sultanates. Arab and Shirazi influences shaped the architecture of towns such as Moroni and Mutsamudu.

history.heading: French rule and independence
paragraphs: France took Mayotte in 1841 and the other three islands by 1886. In a 1974 referendum, three islands voted for independence, which was declared on 6 July 1975, while Mayotte voted to remain French; the Comoros continue to claim Mayotte.

The country has experienced more than 20 coups or attempted coups, several involving the French mercenary Bob Denard. In 1997 Anjouan and Mohéli tried to secede, leading to a new constitution in 2001 that gave each island autonomy within the Union of the Comoros.

culture.heading: Swahili and Islamic culture
paragraphs: Comorian (Shikomori), a language related to Swahili, is spoken by most people; French and Arabic are also official. Almost all Comorians are Sunni Muslims.
The grand mariage, an elaborate and costly wedding ceremony, is central to social status on Grande Comore. The islands are known for producing ylang-ylang, a flower used in perfumes.

politics.heading: Union of the Comoros
paragraphs: The Comoros are a federal presidential republic in which the islands of Grande Comore (Ngazidja), Anjouan (Ndzuwani) and Mohéli (Mwali) each have their own governor. Azali Assoumani, who first came to power in a 1999 coup, has held the presidency for most of the period since, and constitutional changes in 2018 extended his rule. The opposition has boycotted or contested recent elections.

economy.heading: Spices and remittances
paragraphs: The Comoros are among the poorest countries in Africa. Agriculture and fishing dominate, and the islands are leading producers of ylang-ylang essence and vanilla, along with cloves.
Remittances from the diaspora, especially in France, are a vital source of income. Many Comorians try to migrate to Mayotte. The currency is the Comorian franc, pegged to the euro.
